long_form.title_primary: The Connection That Should Never Have Failed
title_challengers: The Shop Drawing That Doomed a Hotel
One Steel Rod Held Two Walkways. Then It Held Four.
long_form.description:
Two walkways hung in a hotel atrium, one above the other. They came down because of a change that made the job easier to build — a routine edit on a shop drawing that quietly doubled the load on a single steel connection. Nobody re-ran the math.

This is a forensic reconstruction of the 1981 Hyatt Regency walkway collapse in Kansas City: the original continuous-rod design, the "as-built" revision that split one rod into two, and why that one change doubled the force on a welded box-beam seam that was already the weakest point in the structure. Analysis, not spectacle — we stay on the steel.

primary.concept: Signature artifact focus (no face — faceless channel). Extreme close-up of a single steel box-beam connection: a threaded rod through a nut bearing on a welded seam, isolated against a dark steel-blue field (>50% negative space). A red circle rings the welded seam; a subtle amber load-arrow pushes up against it. Steel-blue + amber-warning palette, red accent only on the anomaly. Delivers the 'this one joint carried double' promise without showing the collapse or any people.

challengers.concept: Zero-text before/after variant pairing with the 'One Steel Rod Held Two Walkways' title. Split composition on a dark steel-blue field: left, a clean continuous single rod passing through two box beams (as designed); right, the same rod cut into two offset segments (as built), with a red circle on the new upper connection. The delta is visually obvious — one rod becomes two. >50% negative space, no face, amber accent. Tests the mystery-of-the-change angle.

Document-artifact variant pairing with the 'Shop Drawing That Doomed a Hotel' title. A single structural detail drawing seen at an angle in cold light, a revision cloud around the changed connection, a red circle on the initials/approval stamp in the title block. Steel-blue field, >50% negative space, amber accent, no face. Tests the accountability-gap framing against the pure-artifact framing.

long_form.pinned_comment: The part that stays with me: the math that would have caught this takes about a minute to run. The original single-rod design was already on the approved drawing — it would have held. Where do you think the check should have happened: the engineer of record, or the fabricator who proposed the change?
